title: The Life Is in the Blood
sum: Chapter 17 opens the part of Leviticus that scholars call the Holiness Code (chapters 17–26). It makes two demands. First, any ox, sheep or goat slaughtered by an Israelite must be brought to the entrance of the tent of meeting as a peace offering, not killed in an open field, where people had been offering to "goat idols." Second, no one, Israelite or foreigner, may eat blood, because "a body's life is in its blood." Blood belongs to God and is given back on the altar to make atonement.

Wild game may be eaten if its blood is poured out and covered with dirt. Anyone who eats an animal that died on its own or was torn by beasts must wash and is unclean until evening. The chapter sets the pattern for what follows: rules for Israel, many of them binding the foreigner too, backed by the warning "he will be cut off from among his people."
readings: Read as a law of one sanctuary

Every killing of a domestic animal is a sacrifice, done before the LORD. This fits a people camped around one tent. Deuteronomy 12:15–21 later allows ordinary slaughter at home for those who live far from the chosen place, so many readers see the two laws as written for different settings.
Read as a law about life

The core is not the place but the blood. Taking an animal's life is permitted, but its life must be returned to its Maker. Read this way, the chapter teaches reverence for life itself and limits human power over it.

views.H: Moses gave this law in the wilderness, when every Israelite lived near the tent, so all slaughter could be sacrifice. When Israel spread out in the land, Deuteronomy 12 relaxed the rule while keeping the blood ban. The chapter guards against the goat idols worshiped in the desert.
views.C: August Klostermann named chapters 17–26 the Holiness Code in 1877. Many scholars see a separate priestly school (H) that wrote these chapters and edited the older priestly material (P) of chapters 1–16; Israel Knohl argues that H is the later school. Whether the ban on slaughter away from the tent comes before or after Deuteronomy's permission is debated, and so is the date of the chapter.
views.A: Blood is the clearest symbol of the line between life and death. Pouring it out and covering it returns the life to God and keeps the eater from taking in what is not his. Mary Douglas read the rule as part of a larger system in which Israel's table matches its altar.
views.J: Jewish law takes the blood ban from this chapter and Genesis 9:4. Kosher meat is slaughtered by a trained shochet, then soaked and salted to draw out blood (Talmud, Chullin). Covering the blood of a bird or wild animal (kisui hadam, 17:13) is still done with a blessing. The rabbis read 17:11 as the reason sacrifice atones.
views.X: Hebrews quotes the idea of 17:11: "no forgiveness comes about without blood being poured out" (Hebrews 9:22), and sees it fulfilled in Christ's blood. The Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to avoid blood and what was strangled (Acts 15:20, 29), most likely echoing the rules in Leviticus 17–18 for foreigners. Most churches later treated this as a temporary rule for peace between Jewish and Gentile believers; Jehovah's Witnesses apply it to blood transfusions.

deep.b:
In Acts 15 the apostles and elders decide that Gentiles who believe in Jesus need not be circumcised or keep the whole law of Moses. James then names four things they should avoid: food polluted by idols, sexual immorality (porneia), what has been strangled, and blood (Acts 15:20, 29; 21:25). Why these four?

(1) The Leviticus 17–18 reading. Many scholars, including Richard Bauckham, note that these are the very laws Leviticus 17–18 applies to "the foreigner who lives among you": sacrifice to other gods (17:8–9), eating blood (17:10–12), eating animals not properly drained (17:13–15), and the forbidden unions of chapter 18. James, on this reading, asks Gentiles to keep what the Torah itself asks of Gentiles living among Israel.

(2) The Noahide reading. Others connect the list with the laws given to Noah for all humanity, including the blood ban of Genesis 9:4 ("Only, flesh with its life, its blood, you must not eat"). The rabbis later counted seven Noahide laws (Talmud, Sanhedrin 56a).

(3) A rule for table fellowship. Augustine and most later Christians saw the rules as a practical step so that Jewish and Gentile believers could eat together, not as permanent law. Some early Christians, such as the martyrs of Lyon in AD 177, still refused blood. Some manuscripts of Acts (the Western text) drop "strangled" and add the golden rule, which turns the list into purely moral commands: idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed.

echoes: Genesis 9:4–6; Deuteronomy 12:15–27; 1 Samuel 14:32–34; Ezekiel 33:25; Acts 15:20, 29; Acts 21:25; Hebrews 9:22; 1 John 1:7

settings.what: The law of slaughter and blood
settings.to: Aaron and his sons and all the Israelites (17:2), and in 17:8–16 the foreigner living among them
settings.when: For the camp in the wilderness; the opening of the Holiness Code
settings.why: To stop sacrifices to goat-demons in the open field (17:7). Animals fit for sacrifice must be killed at the tent of meeting. No one may eat blood, because the life is in the blood and God has given it for atonement (17:11). Hunters must pour out and cover the blood. The law is spoken to priests and people together because both must keep it.
views: Traditional readers: words of God through Moses at Sinai. Most critical scholars: the work of a priestly Holiness school (H). Knohl and Milgrom date it to the late 700s BC, others to the exile. It widened holiness from the priests to all Israel and the land. The same view applies to chapters 18–26.
Deuteronomy 12:15–16 allows slaughter for food away from the sanctuary. Many read Leviticus 17 as the rule of a small camp. Others read it as a rival law.

traditions.q: Do the blood rules of Leviticus 17 and Acts 15 still apply, even to medicine?
views: Yes. The command to abstain from blood (Acts 15:28–29) applies to taking blood into the body in any way, so members refuse transfusions of whole blood and its main parts. Since 2000, smaller fractions of blood are left to each member's conscience.

The Council of Florence (1442) taught that the apostles' rule on blood was given for a time, to bring Jewish and Gentile believers together, and ended when that reason passed. Giving and receiving blood is a work of charity that can save lives.

The church's ancient canons still forbid eating blood or the meat of strangled animals (Apostolic Canon 63; Council in Trullo, canon 67), so some Orthodox avoid foods like blood sausage. A transfusion is medicine, not food, and is accepted.
Luther wrote that the apostles' rule on blood was a temporary measure of love for the Jewish believers, which no one keeps any longer and no one needs to (On the Councils and the Church, 1539).

title: Not Like Egypt, Not Like Canaan
sum: Chapter 18 is a list of forbidden sexual unions, framed by a warning: do not do what is done in Egypt, where you lived, or in Canaan, where you are going. Keep my rules, "If a human being does them, he will live by them." Then come the close relatives a man may not "expose the nakedness" of: mother, stepmother, sister, granddaughter, aunt, daughter-in-law, sister-in-law, a woman and her daughter, two sisters at once. Then sex during a woman's period, adultery, handing children over to Molech, lying with a male "in the ways of lying down with a woman," and sex with animals.

The chapter ends with a picture of the land itself as a body that "vomits out" people who defile it. The Canaanites did these things and the land spat them out; Israel will be treated the same way. In Jewish practice this chapter is read on the afternoon of Yom Kippur.
readings: Read as family law

Most of the chapter protects the household. In large extended families living close together, these lines kept sex from destroying trust between relatives. The verses on Molech and animals widen the circle to worship and creation.
Read as a boundary for a holy people
The frame (18:1–5, 24–30) says the point is to be unlike other nations. The rules mark out Israel as God's people, and the land enforces them.
Read as moral law for all
Since the land vomited out the Canaanites, who never received the Torah, the rules seem to bind all nations. This is how the rabbis (the Noahide laws) and most Christian tradition have read them.

views.H: These are God's moral laws given at Sinai. They describe real practices around Israel and bind Israel always; many hold that they also express a moral order for all people, since the Canaanites were judged for breaking them.
views.C: Scholars note that chapter 18 addresses the male head of a household and lists women he must not approach; it may draw on older family rules. Chapter 20 repeats many of the same acts with penalties, which suggests two forms of one tradition. The surprising omission of a man's own daughter (implied in 18:17 and by the rabbis) is often discussed.
views.A: Mary Douglas and others read the list as guarding categories: kin from non-kin, human from animal, life-giving fluids from death. Saul Olyan and Jacob Milgrom tie several rules to the waste or mixing of seed. The land vomiting is a body image: the land itself can be made unclean.
views.J: The rabbis call these the arayot, forbidden unions, one of three sins (with idolatry and murder) that a Jew must die rather than commit (Talmud, Sanhedrin 74a). They extended the list with secondary degrees. The Sifra on 18:3 says the practices of Egypt and Canaan included a man marrying a man and a woman marrying a woman. Reading 18 on Yom Kippur afternoon reminds the people that holiness includes the body.
views.X: Paul's condemnation of a man living with his father's wife cites the standard of 18:8 (1 Corinthians 5:1). John the Baptist's rebuke of Herod for marrying his brother's wife rests on 18:16 (Mark 6:18). Henry VIII's annulment case rested on 18:16 (see the note on 20:21). The church's lists of forbidden degrees of marriage grew from this chapter.

deep.b:
Few verses in the Bible are argued over more today. What follows sets out the main readings, each in its strongest form. The site takes no side.

What the Hebrew says. Literally: "And with a male you shall not lie the lyings of a woman; it is to'evah." The plural mishkevei ishah, "lyings of a woman," appears elsewhere only for a woman's sexual experience with a man (Numbers 31:17–18; Judges 21:11–12). The word to'evah, "abhorrent," is used for many things God or people find detestable, from idols to dishonest weights. Leviticus 20:13 adds the death penalty for both men.

The traditional Jewish reading. The rabbis read the verse as a ban on anal intercourse between men, binding on all humanity as one of the Noahide laws (Talmud, Sanhedrin 54a–58a). The Sifra extended the spirit of 18:3 to same-sex marriage. Orthodox Judaism holds this today, while calling for compassion toward gay Jews. Conservative Judaism's 2006 responsum by Rabbis Dorff, Nevins and Reisner kept the biblical ban as they understood it but set aside the rabbinic extensions and allowed same-sex commitment ceremonies; Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism no longer treat the verse as binding.

The traditional Christian reading. The church has read the verse as moral law, not ritual, because it stands among adultery and incest and because the New Testament repeats the judgment. Paul's word arsenokoitai (1 Corinthians 6:9; 1 Timothy 1:10) seems to be built from the Greek of 20:13, arsenos koitēn, "lying with a male" (David F. Wright). Romans 1:26–27 grounds the judgment in creation. The Catholic Catechism calls such acts contrary to natural law while saying gay people must be treated with respect and compassion (§§2357–2359). The Orthodox churches and most evangelical and Pentecostal bodies hold the same view.

Milgrom's limited reading. Jacob Milgrom, a leading Jewish scholar of Leviticus, held that the verse forbids only anal intercourse between men, and that it is addressed to Israelites and residents of the land of Israel, as the frame of chapter 18 suggests. The ban, he thought, says nothing about women or about other forms of intimacy. He suggested the reason was the waste of seed, as with other rules in the chapter.

Olyan's reading. Saul Olyan argued from the phrase "lyings of a woman" that 18:22 originally addressed only the man who takes the active role, and that 20:13 later extended the guilt to both. The concern, he suggested, was a mixing of bodily fluids that defile, tied to purity rather than to same-sex love as we know it.

Brownson and the revisionist case. James Brownson argues that the biblical texts condemn same-sex acts in settings of excess, exploitation, cultic sex and broken gender roles in a culture of honor and shame, and that the deeper biblical logic of "one flesh" is kinship and covenant faithfulness, not the joining of male and female bodies. Christians who accept this reading, including many mainline Protestant churches, conclude that the verses do not address faithful, lifelong same-sex unions. Others point out that Christians no longer keep many nearby laws, such as 18:19 or 19:19, and ask why this one should be kept.

Gagnon's response. Robert Gagnon answers that the verse is absolute in form: it names no setting, no partner's age or status, and no cult. It punishes both partners in 20:13, so it is not only about exploitation. It rests on the creation of humans as "male and female" (Genesis 1:27) and their becoming "one flesh" (Genesis 2:24). The New Testament, he says, sets aside food and purity laws explicitly (Mark 7:19; Acts 10) but repeats the sexual laws, so the comparison with 19:19 fails. Jesus' answer on divorce, "from the beginning of creation he made them male and female" (Mark 10:6; Matthew 19:4–6), is often added. Many traditional scholars, Jewish and Christian, make similar arguments.

The revisionist reply. Revisionists answer that the New Testament also repeats the blood ban of 17:10–14 for Gentile believers (Acts 15:20, 29), which most churches later set aside, and that Ezekiel 18:6 treats the period law of 18:19 as a moral mark too, so repetition alone does not show which laws still bind. They also note that Ezekiel names Sodom's sin as pride, plenty and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49–50). Traditionalists reply in turn that Acts 15 was a temporary rule for table fellowship, while Paul's sexual ethics are grounded in creation.

What everyone agrees on. The verse forbids at least male–male intercourse for Israel, and both partners are punished in 20:13. The disputes are over its reason, its scope, and whether it binds people today.

echoes: Genesis 9:20–27; Genesis 19:4–11; Genesis 35:22; Genesis 38; Deuteronomy 22:30; Deuteronomy 27:20–23; Ezekiel 22:9–11; Mark 6:17–18; Romans 1:24–27; 1 Corinthians 5:1; 1 Corinthians 6:9–11

settings.what: The laws of forbidden sexual unions
settings.to: The Israelites (18:2), spoken to each man as head of a household, and the foreigner living among them (18:26)
settings.when: At Sinai, for life in the land Israel is about to enter
settings.why: To draw lines around the family. It forbids sex with close relatives, sex during a woman's monthly flow, adultery, giving children to Molech, a male with a male, and sex with an animal. The frame names the problem. Do not do as they do in Egypt or in Canaan (18:3), or the land will vomit you out (18:28). The land itself is treated as holy and able to be defiled.
views: Some scholars read it as a ban on one act, anal intercourse between men, perhaps for reasons of purity (Olyan). Others tie it to male status and honor. Milgrom: it bound Israelite men and residents in the land, not all peoples. Others, such as Gagnon and Wenham, read it as a general rule grounded in creation. Churches and synagogues differ; see the note on 18:22.
On 18:21, see the views on the chapter 20 card.

traditions.q: Does 18:22 still forbid same-sex relationships for Christians?
views: Yes. The Catechism teaches that homosexual acts are contrary to natural law and cannot be approved, while people with homosexual tendencies must be accepted with respect and compassion and are called to chastity (Catechism 2357–2359). A 2023 Vatican document, Fiducia Supplicans, allowed brief, unscripted blessings of same-sex couples, though not of their unions, and it caused much debate.
Yes. Marriage is only between a man and a woman, and the Orthodox churches hold the traditional reading of this verse and of Romans 1:26–27.

Lutherans are divided. The Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod holds the traditional reading, while the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America voted in 2009 to allow pastors in committed same-sex relationships, and the Church of Sweden has married same-sex couples since 2009.

Reformed churches are divided. The Presbyterian Church in America and other conservative Reformed churches keep the traditional reading and the Westminster Confession's teaching that marriage is between one man and one woman (24.1). The Presbyterian Church (USA) has allowed gay and lesbian ministers since 2011 and same-sex marriage since 2015.

Anglicans are divided. The Lambeth Conference of 1998 called homosexual practice incompatible with Scripture, but the Episcopal Church has married same-sex couples since 2015 and the Church of England has allowed prayers of blessing since 2023, which many Anglican provinces in Africa and Asia reject.
Methodists are divided. The United Methodist Church removed its bans on gay clergy and same-sex weddings in 2024; the Global Methodist Church, formed in 2022, keeps the traditional teaching.

The Southern Baptist Convention holds that marriage is between one man and one woman and lists homosexual acts among sexual sins (Baptist Faith and Message, articles 15 and 18). A few smaller Baptist groups take the opposite view.

title: Be Holy, Because I Am Holy
sum: "You will be holy, because I am holy." Chapter 19 spells out what that means, and it mixes what modern readers would separate. Honoring parents, keeping Sabbaths, and avoiding idols stand beside eating peace offerings on time. Leaving the edges of the field for the poor stands beside not stealing, not lying, and paying a worker the same day. Do not curse the deaf or trip the blind. Judge fairly, do not spread slander, do not hate your brother in your heart. "You are to love your neighbor as yourself."

The second half adds more: do not mix two kinds of animals, seeds or fabric; wait three years before eating from new fruit trees; do not practice omens or cut and tattoo your bodies for the dead; respect the old; and love the foreigner "as yourself, because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt." Each short command ends with the reason: "I am the LORD."
readings: Read as a holiness of daily life

Holiness here is not only for priests and altars. It reaches the farmer's field, the worker's wages and the courtroom. The God who is holy is also the God who cares for the deaf, the blind and the foreigner.
Read as a commentary on the Ten Commandments

Parents and Sabbath (19:3), idols (19:4), stealing and lying (19:11), the Name (19:12), murder (19:16), adultery (19:20, 29) and coveting (19:18) all appear. A midrash says the chapter contains all ten (Leviticus Rabbah 24:5).

views.H: God spoke these laws at Sinai. The mix of ritual and ethics shows that all of life belongs to God. Many Christians sort them into moral laws that still bind (love, honesty, justice) and ceremonial laws fulfilled in Christ (mixtures, fruit trees).
views.C: The chapter is a collection of short laws, many in groups of two or four, gathered under the call to holiness. Its links with the Ten Commandments and with Deuteronomy suggest a priestly writer rethinking older law. For Milgrom, this chapter is the heart of the Holiness Code, where holiness moves from the sanctuary to the whole people.
views.A: The rules on mixing animals, seeds and fabrics keep creation's categories apart, as Israel is kept apart from the nations. Mary Douglas saw holiness as wholeness and order: each thing in its place. The ban on cutting the body for the dead keeps life and death apart.
views.J: The rabbis called chapter 19, Kedoshim, the place where "most of the essentials of the Torah depend" (Sifra). Rabbi Akiva called 19:18 "a great principle of the Torah." From this chapter come the laws of pe'ah (field corners), orlah (young fruit), sha'atnez (wool and linen), not cutting the corners of the beard, and rising before the elderly. Jewish law forbids tattoos from 19:28.
views.X: Jesus names 19:18 as the second great commandment (Mark 12:31) and tells the parable of the Good Samaritan to answer "Who is my neighbor?" (Luke 10:25–37). Paul and James call it the summary of the law (Romans 13:9; Galatians 5:14; James 2:8). First Peter 1:16 quotes "be holy, because I am holy." Christians debate the tattoo verse: most see it as tied to mourning rites for the dead.

deep.h: Love your neighbor: from Hillel to Paul
deep.b:
The Hebrew of 19:18 is short: ve'ahavta lere'akha kamokha, "and you shall love to your neighbor as yourself." In context the neighbor is a fellow Israelite, "the children of your people," but 19:34 uses the same words for the foreigner.

Hillel. When a would-be convert asked to learn the whole Torah standing on one foot, Hillel answered, "What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. That is the whole Torah; the rest is explanation. Go and learn it" (Talmud, Shabbat 31a). Many see this as Hillel's form of 19:18.

Akiva and Ben Azzai. Rabbi Akiva called 19:18 "a great principle of the Torah." His colleague Ben Azzai named a greater one, Genesis 5:1, because it covers every human being, made in God's likeness, and not only one's neighbor (Sifra; Jerusalem Talmud, Nedarim 9:4).

Jesus. Asked which commandment is first, Jesus gives the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4–5) and then 19:18: "No other commandment ranks above these" (Mark 12:28–34). The scribe who asked agrees. In Luke, the parable of the Samaritan makes a despised outsider the one who acts as neighbor (Luke 10:29–37). In Matthew, Jesus goes further: love your enemies (Matthew 5:43–48).

Paul and James. Paul writes that the commands against adultery, murder, stealing and coveting are summed up in this one word, and "love, then, is what fulfills the law" (Romans 13:8–10; Galatians 5:14). James calls it "the royal law" (James 2:8).

What "as yourself" means. Most read "love your neighbor as you love yourself," as the Greek and the New Testament do, and the Plain text follows them. Others, noting the Hebrew le ("to") and the parallel in 19:34, read "love your neighbor, who is like you" (Naphtali Herz Wessely, Martin Buber). See the note on 19:18.

deep.h: "Fear your God": sins no one sees
deep.b: Twice this chapter adds "Fear your God" to a law: after cursing the deaf and tripping the blind (19:14), and after standing up for the old (19:32). Chapter 25 adds it three more times: for wronging another in a sale, for taking interest, and for ruling harshly over a poor brother (25:17, 36, 43). Rashi, following the Sifra, noticed the pattern: these are matters "handed over to the heart," where only the doer knows his motive. The deaf man does not hear the curse; the borrower cannot prove the lender's intent. No human court could catch these wrongs, so the law appeals to the God who sees.

echoes: Exodus 20:1–17; Exodus 22:21–27; Exodus 23:9; Deuteronomy 24:14–22; Mark 12:28–34; Matthew 5:43–48; Luke 10:25–37; Romans 13:8–10; Galatians 5:14; James 2:1–9; 1 Peter 1:15–16

settings.what: Be holy: holiness in daily life
settings.to: The whole community of the Israelites (19:2): parents, farmers, employers, judges, neighbors and merchants, and the foreigner living among them
settings.when: At Sinai, for life in the land (19:9; 19:23)
settings.why: To show that holiness is not only for priests at the altar. It reaches the harvest, where the edges are left for the poor, and wages, paid the same day. It reaches the court, with no favor to rich or poor, the heart, with no grudge, and the market, with honest weights. Its center is "You are to love your neighbor as yourself" (19:18), with the foreigner included (19:34). Spoken to the whole community, it makes every Israelite answerable for justice.

title: The Penalties
sum: Chapter 20 returns to many of the acts in chapter 18 and gives the penalties. It begins with Molech: whoever gives his children to Molech must be stoned, and if the people look away, God himself will cut him off and his clan. Turning to ghosts and spirits is condemned. Then comes a list: cursing father or mother, adultery, and the forbidden unions, each with its sentence. Several carry death, some "burning," some being "cut off" or dying childless.

The chapter ends as chapter 18 did, with the land that vomits out its people, and with a new reason: "You will be holy for me, because I am holy, I the LORD, and I have set you apart from the peoples to be mine." The clean and unclean animals are part of that separation (20:25).
readings: Read as a criminal code

The chapter sets punishments for a real community. Like other ancient law codes, it uses death to show how serious an offense is. Its focus on the family reflects a society where the household was the base of all life.
Read as a statement of values

Many readers think the death penalties were rarely carried out and served to mark the gravest sins. Read this way, the chapter is less a manual for courts than a scale of how much each wrong offends a holy God.

views.H: God set these penalties for ancient Israel as a nation under his direct rule. They show how serious sin is. Christians in this lens usually hold that the civil penalties ended with Israel's state, while the moral judgments remain.
views.C: Chapter 20 seems to be a parallel collection to chapter 18, arranged by penalty rather than by relative. The Molech law and the warning against ghosts frame the list as a polemic against foreign worship. Critics debate whether the penalties were ever enforced.
views.A: The penalties follow the system of holiness: offenses that confuse the deepest categories, of kin, gender, species and life and death, carry the heaviest sentences. "Their blood is on them" places the guilt on the offender, so the community is not defiled by the execution.
views.J: The rabbis surrounded the death penalty with rules: two eyewitnesses, a warning just before the act, and a court of twenty-three. They also debated how often a court should ever use it, and allowed emergency punishments beyond the letter of the law (see the note on 20:27). The State of Israel has carried out only two executions, most famously that of Adolf Eichmann in 1962.
views.X: Jesus forgave a woman caught in adultery, saying, "The one among you who is without sin should be the first to throw a stone at her" (John 8:7; the passage is missing from the earliest manuscripts). Paul lists many of these sins but tells the church to judge by removing the offender, not by death (1 Corinthians 5:13). Christians have debated whether the state should still use these penalties, from the Puritans to modern theonomists.

deep.h: The death penalties in Leviticus 20 and 24
deep.b:
Leviticus names death for giving children to Molech (20:2), consulting ghosts as a medium (20:27), cursing father or mother (20:9), adultery (20:10), several forms of incest (20:11–12, 14), male–male intercourse (20:13), sex with an animal (20:15–16), blasphemy (24:16) and murder (24:17). How have readers handled these?

The rabbinic way. The rabbis did not deny the penalties but surrounded them with rules: two eyewitnesses, a warning just before the act which the offender had to accept, a full court, and a strong bias toward acquittal (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4–5). The four kinds of execution (stoning, burning, the sword, strangling) were defined so as to be as quick as possible (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:1–3). After the Temple fell, the courts stopped judging capital cases at all. Many rabbis taught that the verses still teach how grave a sin is, though no court can enforce them.

The Christian way. Thomas Aquinas divided the law into moral, ceremonial and judicial parts; the judicial laws, including these penalties, ended with Israel's state (Summa Theologiae I–II q.104). John Calvin and the Westminster Confession say the same: the judicial laws "expired together with the state of that people" (Westminster Confession 19.4). But some Christian states tried to apply them. The Massachusetts Body of Liberties (1641) listed capital crimes with references to Leviticus and Exodus. In the 1970s Greg Bahnsen and the theonomy movement argued that modern states should keep the Mosaic penalties, a view most Christians reject.

Modern debate. Supporters of the death penalty often cite 24:17–21 and Genesis 9:6, where life for life rests on the image of God. Opponents point to the rabbis' strict limits (see the note on 20:27), to Jesus in John 8, and to the Catholic Catechism, which since 2018 calls the death penalty "inadmissible" (§2267).

echoes: Exodus 21:12–17; Exodus 22:18–20; Deuteronomy 13:6–11; Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Deuteronomy 22:22–24; 1 Samuel 28:3–25; 2 Kings 21:6; Ezekiel 18:5–13; John 8:2–11; 1 Corinthians 5:1–13

settings.to: The Israelites (20:2): every Israelite and every foreigner living in Israel. The community, called the people of the land, is to carry out the sentences.
settings.when: At Sinai, for life in the land
settings.why: To give the penalties for the sins of chapter 18, for giving children to Molech and for turning to the dead. Some are for the courts to carry out, others ('I will cut him off') are left to God. The point is that the community cannot look away (20:4–5). It ends with the purpose. Israel is set apart, as the clean animal is set apart from the unclean (20:24–26).
views: Most scholars: child sacrifice to a god Molech (Day; Heider). Eissfeldt: molk was the name of a kind of sacrifice, not a god. Weinfeld: a dedication of children by fire without death. Snaith: children were given over to be raised to serve at a shrine.

title: Priests Without a Defect
sum: Chapters 21–22 turn to the priests. An ordinary priest must not make himself unclean for the dead except for his closest relatives, must not shave his head or cut his body in mourning, and must marry an Israelite woman who is not a prostitute or divorced. A priest's daughter who becomes a prostitute brings shame on her father and is burned. The high priest has stricter rules: he may not mourn even for his father or mother, must not leave the sanctuary, and must marry a virgin of his own people.

Then a list of physical defects: a descendant of Aaron who is blind, lame, has a broken limb, a hunchback, a skin disease, or other defects may not approach the altar to offer "the food of his God." He may still eat the holy food. The reason given is that he must not "treat my holy places as common."
readings: Read as rules for a holy office

The priest stands for the people before God, so his body and household must be whole. The rules are about the office, not the worth of the person: a priest with a defect still eats the holy food and remains a priest.
Read as a hard text about disability
Modern readers, including many with disabilities, find this chapter painful. They ask why God would turn away the lame and the blind, and they read it beside the prophets and Jesus, who welcome them.

views.H: God gave these rules to show that his service requires the best, as sacrificial animals must be without defect. The priest was a living picture of holiness. The rules applied to Aaron's family at the altar, not to Israel as a whole.
views.C: The rules match ideas found in other ancient cultures, where priests had to be physically whole. Some scholars think the strict rules for the high priest reflect the Second Temple, when he was the leader of the people.
views.A: Holiness means wholeness. Animals and priests near the altar must be complete, without blemish, because the altar is the meeting point of God's perfect world and ours. Death is the opposite of holiness, so priests keep away from corpses. Saul Olyan and others have studied how such rules ranked bodies.
views.J: Kohanim, men of priestly descent, still avoid contact with the dead, do not enter cemeteries except for close relatives, and in Orthodox practice may not marry a divorcee or a convert. They bless the people in synagogue with the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24–26). The rabbis listed many defects and said a priest with a visible defect should not bless the people, lest they stare.
views.X: Hebrews calls Christ the high priest who is "holy, free of evil, free of stain, separated from sinners" (Hebrews 7:26), who "offered himself flawless to God" (Hebrews 9:14). Jesus heals the blind and the lame in the Temple (Matthew 21:14) and invites them to the feast (Luke 14:13, 21). Medieval canon law kept some bodily requirements for priests.

echoes: Ezekiel 44:15–31; Malachi 1:6–14; 2 Samuel 5:8; Isaiah 56:3–7; Matthew 21:14; Luke 14:12–24; Hebrews 7:26–28; Hebrews 9:14; 1 Peter 1:19

settings.what: Rules of holiness for priests and the high priest
settings.to: The priests, the sons of Aaron (21:1), and in 21:10–15 the high priest
settings.when: At Sinai, for the priests in all generations
settings.why: To keep the priests fit for their work. They may touch the dead only for close family. They must not shave or cut themselves in mourning, and they must marry within limits. The high priest may not mourn even for his parents and must marry a virgin of his own people. The problem is that priests handle the food of their God, so their holiness affects all Israel (21:8).

settings.to: Aaron (21:17), about his descendants; then told to Aaron, his sons and all the Israelites (21:24)
settings.when: At Sinai, for the priests in all generations
settings.why: To rule that a priest with a defect may eat the holy food but may not serve at the altar. The rule matches the one for animals (22:17–25): what is brought near must be whole. It was told to all Israel so that everyone would know the limits.
views: Many readers see a symbol of wholeness before God, not a judgment on worth. Others find it troubling and read it with Jesus' welcome of the disabled.

title: Holy Food
sum: Chapter 22 guards the holy food. A priest who is unclean, from a skin disease, a discharge, contact with the dead or a creeping thing, must not eat it until he is clean and the sun has set. No outsider may eat it: not a guest, not a hired worker. A slave bought by the priest may eat it, and so may a priest's daughter who is widowed or divorced and childless and has come home. Anyone who eats it by mistake pays it back with a fifth added.

The second half sets rules for the animals offered. They must be without defect for vows and freewill gifts, though a slightly deformed animal may be a freewill gift. A newborn must stay with its mother seven days, and a cow or ewe must not be killed on the same day as its young. The chapter closes: "Do not treat my holy name as common, so that I will be shown to be holy among the Israelites."
readings: Read as temple law
These are working rules for priests: who eats what, when and how. They protect the holy from the common.
Read as a call to honor God's name
The closing verses widen the subject. What priests and people do shows God's holiness to the world, or treats his name as common.

views.H: God gave the priests these rules so that the gifts given to him were treated with reverence, and the people learned that God deserves their best.
views.C: The chapter belongs with 21 as a set of rules for the priesthood, perhaps from the Jerusalem Temple. Malachi's later complaint about blemished offerings (Malachi 1:6–14) shows the rules were not always kept.
views.A: Holy food moves between God, the priest's household and the altar, and the rules map who belongs inside that circle. The mother and young law and the eighth-day rule draw a line between life and death even in sacrifice.
views.J: The command "I will be shown to be holy among the Israelites" (22:32) is the source of kiddush hashem, sanctifying God's name, the duty to live and if need be to die in a way that honors God, and of the ban on chillul hashem, profaning it. The Talmud derives the need for a quorum of ten for some prayers from this verse (Berakhot 21b; Megillah 23b).
views.X: Christ is the lamb "with no flaw and no stain" (1 Peter 1:19). Jesus teaches his followers to pray, "May your name be honored as holy" (Matthew 6:9), the same idea as 22:32.

echoes: Exodus 22:29–30; Deuteronomy 15:21; Deuteronomy 22:6–7; Malachi 1:6–14; Ezekiel 36:20–23; Matthew 6:9; 1 Peter 1:19

settings.what: Who may eat the holy food
settings.when: At Sinai, for the priests in all generations
settings.why: To protect the Israelites' holy gifts. An unclean priest may not eat them. Only the priest's household may eat, including a bought slave but not a hired worker or a daughter married to a layman. A layman who eats by mistake pays it back with a fifth. The problem is keeping holy gifts holy after they leave the altar.

settings.to: Aaron and his sons and all the Israelites (22:18), including the foreigners in Israel who bring offerings
settings.why: To require flawless animals for vows and freewill gifts. A newborn stays with its mother seven days, and a mother and its young are never killed on one day. Lay people choose the animal and priests accept it, so both are told. It ends with the reason: do not treat my holy name as common (22:32).

title: The LORD's Set Times
sum: Chapter 23 is the Torah's fullest list of the feasts, "the LORD's set times." It starts with the weekly Sabbath and then follows the year: Passover on the fourteenth of the first month and the seven days of Unleavened Bread; the waving of the first sheaf of barley "on the day after the Sabbath"; seven weeks counted to the Feast of Weeks, with two loaves of new wheat; the first day of the seventh month, a day of trumpet blasts; the Day of Atonement on the tenth; and the Feast of Booths for seven days from the fifteenth, with a closing assembly on the eighth.

In the middle of the harvest rules comes a reminder: leave the edges of your field for the poor and the foreigner (23:22). The chapter ends with the booths themselves, made with fruit and palm branches, so that every generation will know that God made Israel live in booths when he brought them out of Egypt.
readings: Read as a farmer's calendar
The feasts follow the harvests of the land: barley in spring, wheat seven weeks later, and the fruit and grapes in the fall. Israel gives thanks at each stage.
Read as a calendar of salvation
Passover and Booths remember the exodus and the wilderness. Later tradition linked the Feast of Weeks to the giving of the law at Sinai. The year becomes a retelling of Israel's story.
Read as a picture of God's plan
Many Christians see in the feasts, from Passover to Booths, an outline of Christ's work, from his death and resurrection to Pentecost and his coming again.

views.H: God gave Israel these feasts at Sinai to keep for all time in the land. They are real historical memorials and real thanksgivings. Christians in this lens see them fulfilled, not cancelled, in Christ.
views.C: Exodus 23:14–17 and 34:18–23 name three pilgrimage feasts. Deuteronomy 16 centralizes them. Leviticus 23 adds fixed dates, the Day of Atonement and the first day of the seventh month, which many critics see as a later priestly development. Some think the chapter combines two calendars (23:1–38 and 23:39–43).
views.A: Sacred time, like sacred space, breaks up the ordinary. The feasts mark the turning points of the farming year and of human life, so that the whole cycle of work is offered to God.
views.J: These are the backbone of Jewish life today: Pesach, Shavuot, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Sukkot with Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah. The rabbis set the omer count from the second night of Passover and linked Shavuot with the giving of the Torah. The "day of blasts" became Rosh Hashanah, the New Year. Outside Israel most communities add a second festival day.
views.X: Paul calls Christ "our Passover" (1 Corinthians 5:7) and "the firstfruits" of those raised from the dead (1 Corinthians 15:20). The Spirit came on the Feast of Weeks, Pentecost (Acts 2:1). Jesus taught at the Feast of Booths about living water and light (John 7–8). Colossians 2:16–17 calls festivals "a shadow of the things to come." Some Christians, including Messianic Jews and some Sabbath-keeping churches, still keep the feasts.

deep.h: The feasts in Jewish practice and Christian reading
deep.b:
FeastDateJewish practiceCommon Christian reading
Passover and Unleavened Bread (23:5–8)14–21 of the first monthSeder, matzah, no leavenChrist's death as the Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7); the Lord's Supper
First sheaf (23:9–14)"The day after the Sabbath"Start of the 49-day omer countThe resurrection on the first day of the week (1 Corinthians 15:20)
Feast of Weeks (23:15–21)Fifty days laterShavuot: the giving of the Torah, reading RuthPentecost: the giving of the Spirit (Acts 2)
Day of blasts (23:23–25)1 of the seventh monthRosh Hashanah, the shofarFor some, the final trumpet (1 Thessalonians 4:16)
Day of Atonement (23:26–32)10 of the seventh monthYom Kippur: fasting, confessionChrist's once-for-all offering (Hebrews 9)
Booths (23:33–43)15–22 of the seventh monthSukkah, four species, Simchat TorahGod dwelling with people (John 1:14; Revelation 21:3; Zechariah 14:16)

The Christian readings are traditional, not universal. Many Christians hold that the spring feasts were fulfilled at Christ's first coming and the fall feasts point to his return; others think this reads too much into the calendar. Jews keep the feasts as commands with their own meanings, not as pictures of another story.

The date of the first sheaf was disputed in the Second Temple era. The Pharisees read "the day after the Sabbath" as the day after the first day of Passover; the Sadducees and Boethusians as the day after the weekly Sabbath (Talmud, Menachot 65a–66a). See the variant at 23:11.

deep.h: The poor in the middle of the calendar
deep.b: Verse 22, about leaving the edges of the field, seems out of place between the Feast of Weeks and the day of blasts. Rashi, following the Sifra, asked why it stands among the feasts, and answered that whoever leaves gleanings for the poor is counted as if he had built the Temple and offered his sacrifices in it. It also sits at the very harvest the Feast of Weeks celebrates, so the feast is not complete without the poor and the foreigner. Deuteronomy 16:11, 14 says the same outright, listing the foreigner, orphan and widow among those who rejoice at Weeks and Booths.

echoes: Exodus 12:1–20; Exodus 23:14–17; Exodus 34:18–24; Numbers 28–29; Deuteronomy 16:1–17; Nehemiah 8:13–18; Zechariah 14:16–19; John 7:2, 37–39; Acts 2:1; Acts 3:23; 1 Corinthians 5:7–8; 1 Corinthians 15:20; Colossians 2:16–17

settings.to: The Israelites (23:2): every household, farmer and worker, and those born in Israel who are to live in booths (23:42)
settings.when: Given at Sinai for the land to come: "When you come into the land I am giving you and reap its harvest" (23:10)
settings.why: To fix the holy calendar. It lists the Sabbath, Passover and Unleavened Bread, and the first sheaf. Then come the Feast of Weeks, the day of loud blasts, the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Booths. Each tells the people when to rest, gather and bring offerings. Most of the feasts follow the farming year in the land. Booths also recalls the wilderness (23:43). Moses told the Israelites (23:44), so this is the people's calendar, not only the priests'.
views: Many scholars: the feasts began as harvest festivals and were later tied to the exodus. Traditional readers: they were given at Sinai with both meanings from the start.

title: One Law for All
sum: Chapter 24 begins with the lamp and the bread in the holy place: pure olive oil to keep the lamp burning from evening to morning, and twelve loaves set out on the gold table each Sabbath as a lasting covenant. Then comes a story. The son of an Israelite mother, Shelomith daughter of Dibri, and an Egyptian father fights with an Israelite in the camp and curses the Name. They hold him until God's will is made clear.

God's answer: the one who cursed is to be taken outside the camp, the witnesses lean their hands on his head, and the community stones him. Then the law is stated for all: whoever curses God bears his sin, whoever speaks the Name with contempt must die, and whoever kills a person must die. Injury is repaid in kind: "broken bone for broken bone, eye for eye, tooth for tooth." There is one law for foreigner and native-born alike. The people carry out the sentence.
readings: Read as a court case that makes law
Like the cases in Numbers 9, 15 and 27, a new situation is brought to Moses, who waits for God's ruling. The story shows how law grows from real cases.
Read as a story about belonging
The man is half Egyptian. The ruling makes clear that the same law applies to him as to everyone: the foreigner is neither above the law nor below its protection (24:22).

views.H: This happened in the wilderness. The sentence shows how seriously God treats his name, and the rule of equal law is a basic principle of justice.
views.C: Many scholars think the story was placed here to teach the law that follows, in the style of a legal precedent. The lamp and bread section repeats Exodus 27:20–21 and 25:30 and may have been inserted from another source.
views.A: The name of God stands for God himself. To curse it is to attack the center of the holy system. The witnesses' hands on the head may transfer back the guilt that hearing the curse had placed on them.
views.J: The rabbis read "eye for eye" as money: the value of an eye, not literal maiming (Talmud, Bava Kamma 83b–84a). From 24:16 comes the custom of not saying the four-letter Name aloud. A midrash says Shelomith's name hints that she chatted with everyone, "shalom, shalom," and that her son's father was the Egyptian Moses killed (Leviticus Rabbah 32:4–5; Rashi).
views.X: Jesus quotes "eye for eye" and says, "Do not set yourself against the evil person. Instead, when someone slaps your right cheek, turn the other one to him as well" (Matthew 5:38–39). Most Christians read this as a rule for personal revenge, not a cancellation of fair courts. Jesus was charged with blasphemy (Mark 14:64), and Stephen was stoned outside the city on the same charge (Acts 6:11; 7:58).

deep.b:
The rule of equal payback, lex talionis, appears three times in the Torah (24:19–21; Exodus 21:23–25; Deuteronomy 19:21). Older law codes have it too: the Code of Hammurabi says that if a man puts out the eye of a free man, his own eye is put out (laws 196–200), though a commoner's eye cost only silver. Leviticus makes it equal for all: "one law for foreigner and native-born alike."

Many scholars think the rule limited revenge rather than requiring it: no more than an eye for an eye. The rabbis, noting that no two eyes are equal, ruled that payment is in money (Talmud, Bava Kamma 83b–84a), and Josephus says the injured person could accept money (Antiquities 4.280). Philo took it literally. Jesus calls his followers beyond it, to not taking revenge at all (Matthew 5:38–42). Among Christians, Augustine and Aquinas taught that the rule still guides just punishment by the state.

deep.title: Claude's theory: why a story here?
deep.b: Leviticus is almost all law; besides the ordination of the priests (chapters 8–9), its only stories are this one and the death of Nadab and Abihu (chapter 10). These two are about the holy name and the holy place being treated with contempt, and both end in death. Mary Douglas (Leviticus as Literature) explained the placement of chapter 24 by the book's ring structure. My further suggestion is that the story of the half-Egyptian son is placed right before chapter 25's laws of release on purpose. The man belongs to Israel through his mother but stands outside through his father. The verdict, "one law for foreigner and native-born," prepares the reader for chapter 25, where the line between Israelite and foreigner becomes the hardest question in the book: who may be held as a slave for good (25:44–46)?

echoes: Exodus 21:23–25; Exodus 22:28; Exodus 25:30; Exodus 27:20–21; Numbers 9:6–14; Numbers 15:32–36; Numbers 27:1–11; Deuteronomy 19:21; 1 Kings 21:10–13; Matthew 5:38–42; Matthew 26:65; Acts 7:58

settings.what: The oil for the lamp and the bread of the Presence
settings.to: The Israelites, who supply the oil and flour (24:2), and Aaron, who keeps the lamps and the bread (24:3–9)
settings.when: At Sinai, for the tent of meeting, always
settings.why: To keep the lamp burning, and to set the twelve loaves on the table before the LORD every Sabbath. The people's gifts sit in God's presence as a covenant for all time (24:8), and the bread then goes to the priests.

settings.what: The ruling on cursing God and on injury
settings.to: Moses and the Israelites (24:15), about the son of an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father who had cursed the Name; the whole community is to carry out the sentence
settings.when: In the camp at Sinai, after the case was brought to Moses (24:10–12)
settings.why: To decide a case the law had not covered. The text says only that they waited for the LORD's word (24:12). Many readers think the question was whether someone with a foreign father came under Israel's law. The answer is one law for foreigner and native-born alike (24:22). It covers cursing God, and murder and injury, eye for eye. The rule of equal penalty limits revenge as much as it demands justice.
views: Rabbinic law and many modern scholars: in practice the rule set payment equal to the loss. Others think it was meant literally at first.

title: Proclaim Release in the Land
sum: Chapter 25 is spoken "on Mount Sinai." Every seventh year the land is to rest: no sowing or pruning, and what grows on its own is food for everyone. After seven times seven years, on the Day of Atonement of the fiftieth year, the ram's horn sounds and the Jubilee begins. "Proclaim release in the land for all who live in it." Each family goes back to its own land, because land cannot be sold for good: "the land is mine. You are foreigners and lodgers living with me."

Land sales are priced by the years left to the Jubilee, and a relative may redeem the land at any time. Houses in walled cities may be sold permanently after a year; Levite houses are always redeemable. If a brother grows poor, help him; lend without interest. If he sells himself to you, treat him like a hired worker, not a slave, and free him at the Jubilee, "because they are my servants." But foreigners may be bought as permanent slaves. If an Israelite is sold to a foreigner, his family must buy him back.
readings: Read as economic law
The chapter builds a reset into the economy, so that poverty and land loss never become permanent. It is one of the most ambitious social laws of the ancient world.
Read as a theology of ownership
Two claims drive it: the land belongs to God (25:23) and the people belong to God (25:42, 55). Every rule follows from these. Human ownership is always borrowed.
Read as hope
Since no record shows the Jubilee being kept, prophets, Qumran and the New Testament turned it into a picture of a coming age of release.

views.H: God gave Israel a law meant to be kept in the land. If it was neglected, as 26:34–35 and 2 Chronicles 36:21 suggest, the fault lay with Israel, not with the law. It shows God's care for the poor and his ownership of all things.
views.C: Many critics see the Jubilee as a priestly reform program, perhaps from the exile or after, with roots in older debt releases. Others see an early tribal ideal. The relationship with Exodus 21 and Deuteronomy 15, which release Hebrew slaves after six years, is a major question.
views.A: The Jubilee is a ritual of return: everything goes back to its place, as creation returns to Sabbath rest. Time, like space, has its holy center, and the economy is brought back to its original order every fifty years.
views.J: The rabbis held that the Jubilee lapsed when the tribes east of the Jordan were exiled, and with it the full force of the Sabbath year (Talmud, Arakhin 32b). The Sabbath year is still observed in Israel by rabbinic law. Hillel's prozbul let lenders collect debts despite the seventh-year release, so that the poor could still get loans (Mishnah Sheviit 10:3–4).
views.X: Jesus' first sermon in Luke reads Isaiah 61, a Jubilee text, and announces its fulfillment (Luke 4:16–21). The early church shared goods so that "nobody among them was in need" (Acts 4:34), echoing Deuteronomy 15:4. The Catholic Church has held Jubilee years since 1300. Christian justice movements, such as the Jubilee 2000 campaign for debt relief, took their name from this chapter.

deep.b:
No passage in the Bible describes a Jubilee being proclaimed. Here are the main views.

It was kept for a time, then lapsed. The rabbis held that it was observed while all the tribes lived in the land (Sifra; Talmud, Arakhin 32b), and counted Jubilees for dating. Some modern scholars, such as Robert North, think it reflects real early practice.

It reformed real practice. Moshe Weinfeld showed that kings in Mesopotamia proclaimed releases, andurāru (the Akkadian cousin of deror, 25:10) and mīšarum, canceling debts and freeing debt slaves, often at the start of a reign. The Jubilee turns that royal act into a fixed law under God, the true king. Zedekiah's slave release (Jeremiah 34:8–17) and Nehemiah's debt release (Nehemiah 5:1–13) show such acts in Israel.

It was an ideal. Julius Wellhausen and many since think it was a late priestly program that was never put into practice, a utopia that criticized land grabbing (Isaiah 5:8; Micah 2:2).

It became a hope. John Bergsma traces how later writers turned the Jubilee into a picture of the end: Isaiah 61, Daniel's seventy weeks (seventy sevens of years, Daniel 9:24), the book of Jubilees, which dates all history in 49-year periods, and 11QMelchizedek, which pictures a final Jubilee of release. Luke 4 belongs to this stream.

The idea has had a long life. Pope Boniface VIII proclaimed the first Catholic Holy Year in 1300; Jubilee years are now held every twenty-five years, and Pope John Paul II linked the Jubilee of 2000 with a call to cancel the debts of poor nations (Tertio Millennio Adveniente 51, 1994). The Jubilee 2000 campaign, led by churches and aid groups, pressed rich countries to forgive debts and helped bring about debt relief for many of the poorest countries. Liberation theologians, Christian Anabaptists such as John Howard Yoder, and Jewish social justice groups use the Jubilee to argue for land reform and limits on inherited wealth. Critics, both conservative and some biblical scholars, warn that a law for tribal land in Canaan cannot simply be turned into modern economic policy; defenders answer that its principles, that the earth is God's and that poverty must not become permanent, still apply.

In American history the KJV of 25:10 on the Liberty Bell became an abolitionist slogan, even as defenders of slavery cited 25:44–46. Both sides read this chapter.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the Jubilee undoes Joseph's Egypt
deep.b: In Genesis 47:13–26, during the famine, Joseph buys all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, and the people sell themselves into Pharaoh's service in exchange for food; only the priests keep their land. Leviticus 25 reads like the opposite. In Israel the land cannot be sold for good, because it is God's, not a king's. Israelites cannot be sold as slaves, because they are God's servants. And the priestly tribe, Levi, is given special rights to redeem its houses. Commentators often note the contrast with Egypt in 25:42 and 25:55; the specific link to Genesis 47 is my suggestion. On this reading the writer meant Israel to be a reverse Egypt in its economy as well as its worship: the God who brought them out of "the house of slaves" will not let them rebuild it among themselves (25:38, 42, 55).

echoes: Exodus 21:1–11; Exodus 23:10–11; Deuteronomy 15:1–18; Ruth 4:1–10; 1 Kings 21:1–3; Isaiah 5:8; Isaiah 61:1–2; Jeremiah 32:6–15; Jeremiah 34:8–22; Nehemiah 5:1–13; Ezekiel 46:16–18; Luke 4:16–21; Acts 4:32–35

settings.what: The Sabbath year and the Jubilee
settings.by: The LORD, speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai
settings.to: The Israelites (25:2), as landowners, farmers, lenders and masters. The law also concerns the poor brother who sells land or himself (25:25; 25:39).
settings.when: For the future: "When you come into the land that I am giving you" (25:2)
settings.why: To keep the land and the people from being bought up for good. Every seventh year the land rests. The fiftieth year is proclaimed on the Day of Atonement. Then land goes back to its family and Israelite slaves go free. Close kin are to buy back what a poor relative sold. The reason is given. The land is God's, and the Israelites are foreigners and lodgers living with him (25:23). The problem is poverty and debt that pass from one generation to the next.
views: Some scholars think the Jubilee was a utopian program, never fully practiced. Others argue it was a workable early law (North; Bergsma), or that it reflects real ancient release decrees (Weinfeld).

title: Blessings, Curses and the Promise
sum: After a reminder, no idols, keep my Sabbaths, fear my holy place, God sets out the covenant's two paths. If Israel walks in his rules: rain in its season, harvest following harvest, peace, victory, many children, and above all, "I will set my dwelling among you... I will walk about among you. I will be your God, and you will be my people." God broke the bars of their yoke and made them walk upright.

If they will not listen: terror, disease, defeat, drought, wild beasts, war, plague and famine, each stage "seven times" worse, until parents eat their children, cities lie in ruins, and the people are scattered among the nations. Then the land will rest and "make up for its Sabbaths." Yet when they confess and their hearts are humbled, God will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham, and remember the land. "Even while they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject them."
readings: Read as covenant sanctions
Like ancient treaties, the covenant ends with blessings and curses. They show what is at stake in keeping or breaking it.
Read as prophecy
The curses describe the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles with striking detail. Traditional readers see Moses foretelling them; Jews have read the long exile after AD 70 through this chapter too.
Read as a call to return
The curses come in stages, each one meant to turn the people back before the next. The chapter ends not in judgment but in a promise that God will not let go.

views.H: Moses gave this warning at Sinai, and Israel's later history fulfilled it. The chapter's closing promise shows God's faithfulness even when Israel fails.
views.C: Most critical scholars date at least the exile section (26:33–45) to the time of the Babylonian exile or after, because it describes the land's desolation and the people's confession so closely. Milgrom dated most of the chapter earlier, to the eighth century, when Assyria's deportations were known. The many links with Ezekiel suggest the two come from the same priestly circles.
views.A: The land is a living party to the covenant: it vomits out (18:28), it rests, it makes up for its Sabbaths (26:34), and God remembers it (26:42). Blessing is order: rain, fruit and peace in their seasons; curse is that order falling apart.
views.J: The curses, called the Tokhechah, are read in an undertone without a break (Talmud, Megillah 31b). The chapter's last verses are a mainstay of Jewish hope: "I will not reject them" is read as a promise that God sent leaders in every age of exile (Megillah 11a). Ramban saw the chapter as foretelling the first exile and Deuteronomy 28 the second.
views.X: Paul quotes 26:11–12 to call the church God's temple (2 Corinthians 6:16), and Revelation 21:3 hears its fulfillment at the end. Paul's "did God push his people away? By no means!" (Romans 11:1) echoes 26:44. Stephen accuses his hearers of "uncircumcised hearts" (26:41; Acts 7:51). Christians debate whether the blessings and curses apply to nations today.

deep.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls and Leviticus 17–27
deep.b: Chapters 17–27 are well attested at Qumran. The Paleo-Hebrew Leviticus scroll from Cave 11 (11QpaleoLev-a), written in the old Hebrew script, preserves parts of chapters 18–27; 4QLev-e and 11QLev-b preserve smaller pieces; and 4QLXXLev-a is a Greek copy of 26:2–16. Their editors report that the scrolls mostly agree with the Masoretic Text, with a number of small agreements with the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint (D. N. Freedman and K. A. Mathews, 1985). The longest difference in this part, the plus at 17:4, is supported by 4QLev-d. Variant entries are given here only where a reading changes the sense.

Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 are the Torah's two great lists of covenant curses. Leviticus speaks in God's first person ("I will...") and moves in five rising stages (26:14–17, 18–20, 21–22, 23–26, 27–39), each beginning with refusal to listen. Its climax is exile and the land's rest.

The later Bible reads its history through this chapter. Second Kings 17 explains the fall of Samaria as covenant breaking. Jeremiah's seventy years of exile are joined to 26:34 in 2 Chronicles 36:21: the exile lasted "until the land had made up for its Sabbaths." Daniel 9 begins with Jeremiah's seventy years, offers the confession that 26:40 calls for, and receives the answer of "seventy weeks" (Daniel 9:2–24). Nehemiah 9 and Ezra 9 are confessions in the same pattern. Ezekiel shares many of the chapter's words: "staff of bread," "dung-idols," sword, plague and famine, and a "covenant of peace" (Ezekiel 34:25–30).

Ancient treaties are a close parallel. The Vassal Treaties of Esarhaddon of Assyria (672 BC) curse rebels with iron ground and bronze sky, plague and starvation to the point of eating their children. Scholars debate how much Israel's curse lists borrow from such treaties.

The hardest question is what the curses say about God. Some readers find in them a God who punishes harshly; others stress that every stage aims to bring the people back, and that the chapter's last word is God's refusal to break his covenant (26:44–45).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the land as a third partner
deep.b: In most covenants there are two parties. In Leviticus 17–26 the land behaves like a third. It has Sabbaths owed to it (25:2–5). It can be made unclean and vomit out those who defile it (18:25–28; 20:22). It can "enjoy" or "make up for" its rest (26:34, 43). And when God remembers his covenant with the fathers, he adds, "and the land I will remember" (26:42). Jan Joosten (People and Land in the Holiness Code, 1996) and Jacob Milgrom have stressed the land's role in these chapters. My further suggestion is that the Holiness Code treats the land almost as a person with rights, and that the exile is presented less as Israel's punishment than as the land being repaid what it was owed. This would explain why the curses climax not in Israel's suffering but in the land's rest.

echoes: Exodus 6:6–7; Exodus 23:20–33; Deuteronomy 28; Deuteronomy 30:1–10; 1 Kings 8:33–53; 2 Kings 17:7–23; 2 Chronicles 36:20–21; Jeremiah 29:10–14; Ezekiel 34:25–31; Ezekiel 37:26–27; Daniel 9:1–19; Romans 11:1–2, 25–29; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Revelation 21:3

settings.what: The blessings, the curses and the promise
settings.by: The LORD, through Moses on Mount Sinai (26:46)
settings.to: The Israelites, the people who will live in the land
settings.when: The close of the laws given at Sinai, looking ahead to life in the land and beyond it
settings.why: To press the people to keep the covenant. If they obey, there will be rain, peace and God walking among them. If they do not, there will be disease, defeat and exile. Its curses resemble those of Assyrian treaties (Wiseman). It does not end with exile. If they confess, God will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham. The land will rest its missed Sabbaths (26:40–45). For readers who had lost the land, it explained why and gave them hope.
views: Traditional readers: a prophetic warning given at Sinai. Many critical scholars: written in the light of the exile of 587 BC. Milgrom and others: older than Ezekiel, who borrows its language. On this view it was shaped by the Assyrian exile of the north.

title: Gifts Given to God
sum: The book ends with an appendix on gifts. A person may vow the value of a human being to God; the price is fixed by age and sex, from fifty shekels for a man in his prime to three for a baby girl, and a poor man pays what the priest says he can. An animal fit for sacrifice, once vowed, is holy and may not be swapped. An unfit animal, a house or a field may be valued and redeemed, with a fifth added. Fields are priced by the seed they take and the years left to the Jubilee.

Some things cannot be vowed, because they already belong to God: firstborn animals and anything "devoted." A devoted person may not be ransomed. Every tithe of the land and every tenth animal that passes under the rod is holy to the LORD. The book's last words: "These are the commands that the LORD gave Moses for the Israelites on Mount Sinai."
readings: Read as sanctuary finance
The chapter regulates income for the sanctuary: vows paid in silver, redeemed property, tithes. It makes worship practical.
Read as a fitting end
After blessings and curses, the book closes with people giving freely. The covenant ends not with threat but with offering.

views.H: God gave Moses these rules on Sinai along with the rest. They regulate the voluntary gifts of a grateful people.
views.C: Since 26:46 reads like a closing line, many scholars think chapter 27 was added later, perhaps to link the Jubilee laws with the sanctuary's income. Its rules on tithes differ from those in Numbers 18 and Deuteronomy 14.
views.A: Vows move persons and things from the common to the holy, and redemption moves them back with a payment. The chapter maps the border between what is ours and what is God's.
views.J: The tractate Arakhin ("Valuations") works out this chapter, and Temurah the rule on exchanges. The rabbis discouraged rash vows; the Kol Nidre prayer on the eve of Yom Kippur annuls vows people could not keep. When the reading of Leviticus is finished, the congregation calls out "Be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened."
views.X: Jesus warned against vows that dodge duty to parents (Mark 7:9–13) and told his followers to let their yes be yes (Matthew 5:33–37). Thirty shekels, the value of a woman in 27:4 and of a slave in Exodus 21:32, was the price paid to Judas (Matthew 26:15). Christians debate whether the tithe of 27:30–32 binds the church.

echoes: Numbers 6:1–21; Numbers 18:14–28; Numbers 30; Deuteronomy 14:22–29; Deuteronomy 23:21–23; Judges 11:30–40; 1 Samuel 1:11, 27–28; Ecclesiastes 5:4–6; Malachi 3:8–10; Matthew 5:33–37; Mark 7:9–13; Matthew 26:15

settings.to: The Israelites (27:2): anyone who vows a person's value, an animal, a house or a field to the LORD. The priest sets some values.
settings.when: At Sinai, for the sanctuary and for life in the land; the closing words (27:34) end the book
settings.why: To answer what happens when someone promises God more than an animal, such as the worth of a person or a field. The law fixes a value by age and sex (27:3–7). The priest sets one for the poor, for animals and for houses (27:8; 27:12; 27:14). A field is valued by its seed and the years until the Jubilee. The giver may often buy back a gift by adding a fifth. Firstborn animals and things devoted to the LORD cannot be vowed, because they are his already. Tithes are holy to the LORD too, though a tithe of produce may be bought back with a fifth (27:31). The problem is rash or large promises to God and how to keep them honestly.
views: Many scholars: chapter 27 was added after chapter 26 had ended the Holiness Code. Others see it placed on purpose, closing the book with what Israel gives back to God.

traditions.q: Are Christians required to give a tithe, a tenth of their income?
views: Catholics must help provide for the needs of the Church, each according to their ability, but no fixed tenth is required today (Catechism 2043). Tithes were once collected by law in Catholic Europe.

Christians are free from the tithe law of Moses; giving is a joyful response to the gospel (2 Corinthians 9:7). Many Lutheran churches encourage giving a growing share of income, with the tithe as a goal rather than a rule.

Many Baptist churches teach the tithe as the starting point of Christian giving. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000) asks believers to give cheerfully, regularly, systematically, in proportion to their income, and generously.
The tithe belongs to God, and Adventists return a tenth of their income to the church, besides offerings, as a part of faithful stewardship (Fundamental Beliefs 21).
Paying a tithe of one tenth of one's increase is a commandment given by modern revelation (Doctrine and Covenants 119), and it is required for entering the temple.
